column4: One pilgrim asks only for worldly benefit and consequently has no share in the afterlife, closely matching the worldly tilth with no afterlife portion in 42:20.
The contrasting prayer asks for good in both the world and the afterlife, refusing to make the nearer field the sole crop.
Those who ask for both goods receive a share of what they have earned, joining labor, portion, and lasting outcome.
Cultivated land is listed among the alluring provisions of worldly life, making the field itself one object of the preference named in 87:16.
What is better than those worldly attractions is then identified as abiding gardens with the Lord, turning cultivation toward its lasting end.
The idolaters assign invented portions of crops to God and partners, a precise corruption of the harvest's true due.
God is said to accept repentance and take charities, identifying the Lord as the ultimate receiver of the share released from wealth.
Those who desire worldly life and its adornment are paid their works in full here, a crop intentionally confined to the nearer field.
For those worldly workers nothing remains in the afterlife but fire and their works become void, stating the failed permanence of that harvest.
God spreads the earth and causes every well-balanced thing to grow in it, joining cultivation to fitting measure.
God's treasuries release everything only in a known measure, closely matching the section's measured outgoing share and divine provision.
Full measure and just weight are commanded and called better in outcome, clarifying how a due is paid without corrupting the remainder.
The faithful neither squander nor withhold when spending but keep a measured middle, a boundary around both the paid share and what remains.
God-given wealth is to seek the afterlife while retaining one's worldly share and avoiding corruption, a direct statement of how one provision is sown toward the lasting field.
God is said to have caused human beings to grow from the earth as a plant, extending the section's cultivated growth to the person who purifies himself.
Woe is declared for those who defraud in measure, the commercial opposite of giving the produce's rightful portion.
The defrauders demand full measure when receiving from others, exposing grasping at the incoming share.
When measuring or weighing for others they diminish it, directly reversing payment of the known due.
The condemned person gathers wealth and repeatedly counts it, holding the whole yield rather than releasing its claim.
He imagines that his wealth makes him permanent, the false worldly version of the section's abiding good.
Rain brings fruits from the earth as provision, a compact divine field scene in which the product is received rather than self-created.
Those who spend without reminders or injury retain their reward, specifying conduct by which a gift's fruit is not spoiled.
A kind word and forgiveness are better than charity followed by injury, marking a boundary between cleansing gift and morally damaged gift.
Mary's Lord accepts her graciously and makes her grow with good growth, an explicit human counterpart to divinely blessed cultivation.
Those who withhold God's bounty mistake stinginess for good, but what they hoard becomes a burden, reversing the good remainder produced by giving.
Worldly enjoyment is called little and the afterlife better for the God-fearing, tying the better field to the same fearing stance as 87:10.
Worldly life is play and diversion while the afterlife home is better for those who fear, another specific statement of the two valuations behind the field choice.
Those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend it are warned, a concrete reversal of wealth released in purification.
The addressees are asked whether they are content with worldly life instead of the afterlife and are told its enjoyment is slight.
The afterlife home is called better for those who fear, repeating the link between fear and the better lasting destination.
People rejoice in worldly life even though it is only a passing enjoyment beside the afterlife, distinguishing temporary provision from final gain.
God sends down water and brings out fruits as provision, assigning the field's useful yield to its Lord.
God places livelihoods on earth for people and for creatures they do not provide for, widening the beneficiaries of the measured growth in 15:19.
Fertilizing winds and water from heaven are supplied while humans do not control its stores, locating crop growth in divine husbandry.
Those receptive to their Lord's revelation are promised good here and a better home in the afterlife, repeating the better destination of good action.
Whoever wants the immediate life receives only what God chooses before reaching a destructive end, defining one deliberately short-term cultivation.
Whoever seeks the afterlife with fitting effort and faith has that effort appreciated, the active counterpart to sowing for the afterlife.
The prohibition on squandering immediately after giving each claimant his due prevents payment of the share from becoming waste.
David and Solomon judge a crop damaged at night by sheep, a concrete boundary of responsibility around cultivated yield.
Rain makes the earth green under God's subtle care, a concise image of hidden provision becoming visible growth.
God sends pure water from heaven, placing purity itself at the source of the revival described in the next ayah.
That water revives dead land and gives drink to animals and people, joining purification, growth, and provision.
The command to give full measure and not be among those who diminish restates the justice required when a known portion leaves one's goods.
Straight weighing specifies the honest measurement by which the due is separated.
People's goods must not be diminished and the earth must not be corrupted, extending just measurement into the care of the ground itself.
Rain brings forth fruits of varied colors, another direct formulation of the Lord producing the field's yield.
Water descends in a measured amount and revives dead land, linking measure, provision, and renewed growth.
Provision descends from heaven and revives the earth after death, making the productive field one of the signs to be understood.
People are commanded to spend from provision before death makes them wish for time to give charity, placing a firm limit on when the share can bear fruit.
The righteous give desired food to the poor, orphan, and captive, turning provision itself into the released share.
They feed only for God's face and seek neither repayment nor thanks, matching the purified giver's motive in 92:20.
